title: 'It was devastating': Superannuation lost to dodgy switching schemes
text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic:Superannuation

Regulators and consumer advocates have warned Australians scammers are targeting their retirement savings. (Unsplash: Andre Taissin)

Telemarketers who cold call people trying to convince them to switch super providers will need to be licensed.

Unlicensed telemarketers who cold call and make unsolicited approaches to convince people to switch their super will be banned under long-awaited reforms.

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino will appear at the National Press Club today and announce a suite of reforms to better protect Australians from operators that rob them of their retirement savings.

The reforms follow the collapse of the Shield and First Guardian funds, which saw 12,000 people lose more than $1 billion in retirement savings and exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia's almost $4.5 trillion retirement savings pool.

Currently, people might go on Facebook and click an ad that looks innocent, like "Find Your Lost Super" or "Check Your Super", but then gives permission for a telemarketer, also known as a "lead generator", to contact them and suggest they connect with a financial adviser to switch their super.

Mr Mulino said that, under the changes, lead generators would need to be licensed to advertise.

Daniel Mulino will present superannuation reforms at National Press Club. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

It stops short of the outright ban on advertising that some consumer groups have been calling for.

The assistant treasurer said there would be "exceptions" to protect advocacy, educational and employment communications.

The collapses of the First Guardian and Shield schemes have exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia's $4.3 trillion superannuation sector.

"They target the point at which consumers are first exposed to harm and reduce the ability of bad actors to gain access to consumers in the first place."

Mr Mulino said he also wanted to "strengthen the anti‑hawking regime to enhance consent requirements, limit the existing financial advice exemption to existing client relationships and strengthen penalties for breaches".

That would require licensees "to take reasonable steps to ensure lead generation activities comply with relevant regulatory and legal requirements".

Michael Johnson is one of thousands of investors who lost his retirement savings, along with his wife, Caroline, when First Guardian collapsed in April 2025.

They each had separate superannuation accounts with retail funds, but in October 2020 moved about $500,000 of their super from APRA-regulated funds into one joint self-managed superannuation fund (SMSF).

Michael Johnson and his wife lost $500,000 of their retirement savings. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Mr Johnson said he decided to switch his super after seeing an advertisement on Facebook and then being contacted by a lead generator, who eventually put him in touch with financial advisers at United Global Capital (UGC).

ASIC is investigating whether lead generators are complying with their legal obligations when suggesting people switch their retirement savings into less-regulated investment schemes.

That call from the telemarketer quickly led him to connect with financial advisory firm UGC, which convinced him and his wife to move all their super and invest it wholly in the First Guardian Master Fund.

UGC entered liquidation in August 2024, and ASIC cancelled the advisory firm's Australian Financial Services Licence (AFSL) in July 2024.

The primary adviser from UGC involved was contacted for comment but did not respond.

Mr Johnson said the financial advisers "were very convincing", but that had the government-regulated lead generators not been there before he and his wife switched their super, "we wouldn't have gone in at all".

Telemarketers, also known as lead generators, contact people after the click on social media ads and give their contact details. (iStock: Tero Vesalainen)

"Part of how this worked was a remarkably large number of people signing up at the same time," Mr Johnson said.

Mr Johnson said at the time he invested, First Guardian was described to the couple as a "diversified" investment vehicle.

He didn't realise anything was wrong until it was too late.

The assistant treasurer is looking to revamp funding for the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, saying that large super funds, as well as people with self-managed super funds (SMSFs), could be asked to chip in.

"It was devastating," Mr Johnson told ABC News.

"We're approaching retirement. Caroline was looking at reducing her work hours. We wanted to be able to retire and keep our current lifestyle."

Mr Johnson said the couple no longer knew how they could manage financially.

"It looks like we will be needing to have a government pension and the whole point of having compulsory superannuation is that you don't need [to do] that," he said.

Super Consumers CEO Xavier O'Halloran supports the ban on unlicensed cold calling, but wants to see obligations on social media platforms to take down harmful ads.

A review of nine online trading companies finds several are encouraging Australians to jump on "complex" deals, putting them at risk of major losses.

He said that through lead generators, consumers' details were then sold to a financial advisor, "where you're put into really a train towards selling you financial advice, often quite expensive, over $10,000 in some cases, and getting you to switch into certain products".

"We still want to see greater protections and obligations on the social media platforms to ensure that these ads are taken down if there are still harmful ones being put up," he said.

Xavier O'Halloran wants to see obligations on social media platforms to take down harmful ads. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"We don't want to see claims made that can't be substantiated. We don't want to see people's details collected then on-sold to someone else without their knowledge.

"We don't want … what is meant to be a basic health check on their superannuation, then suddenly sold into very expensive financial advice that sees them switched into really inappropriate products and have their entire retirement savings wiped out."

Today, Mr Mulino is also expected to announce changes to the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort (CSLR), which covers victims of financial misconduct who have not been compensated for their losses — up to $150,000.

He is expected to broaden the number of sectors that pay the levy to fund the scheme, including big super funds.

The "but for" test, which considers whether a claimant would have been in a better financial position had they received appropriate advice and earned interest, is expected to be removed.

The "but for" test has faced criticism from some in the advice industry for using a definition that's too broad, but consumer groups argue that removing it punishes victims of misconduct.

Stronger obligations on super platforms to check the investments they offer and act when things go wrong are also anticipated, along with stronger powers for ASIC to make platforms pay if they fail to protect their customers.

Mr Mulino is expected to unveil financial advice reforms to make financial advice more affordable and accessible to a broader range of consumers.

Michael Johnson said he and his wife, Caroline, had made a complaint to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) to recover their super lost in the First Guardian collapse, but the body was still investigating their claim.

If their claim fails, or if AFCA cannot recover the money from UGC, the couple will have to rely on the CSLR.

The CSLR will treat the couple's claims as one claim, and the $150,000 cap falls well short of their total losses.

Mr Johnson said if their retirement money had stayed in performing superannuation funds, he estimated that, together, they would have accumulated about $1.3 million in retirement savings by now.

Super Consumers' Mr O'Halloran was concerned removing the "but for" test would punish consumers and urged victims of the First Guardian and Shield collapses to claim before it is removed.

"For a typical person that was invested in Shield and First Guardian — if they don't get their complaint in by July 1 of 2027 — they could miss out on any investment earnings that they would have otherwise received in compensation," he said.

Mr O'Halloran said people who lost their life savings in the Shield and First Guardian collapses lost an average of $100,000, and Super Consumers' modelling found the government's proposed change could cost them another $26,500 in lost investment earnings.

Mary Delahunty, chief executive of the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA), welcomed the changes to ensure unlicensed lead generation operators were banned.

But she was unhappy that super funds were being tapped to pay for growing claims under the CSLR.

"What that amounts to is like a tax on every Australian to pay for a scheme that, yes, needs to exist, but not in its unsustainable form.

"So this is an ongoing point that we need to work with the government on."

Mary Delahunty says super funds should not be tapped to pay for the CSLR levy. (ABC News: Paul Pandoulis)

Sarah Abood, CEO of the Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA), welcomed the minister's expected change to broaden the scope of financial advice consumers can access.

"Australians need a financial advice system that is affordable, accessible and trustworthy."
